beats.heading: COLD OPEN
beats.text: On the morning of September twenty-second, nineteen eighty, Iraqi aircraft attacked Iranian airfields. Ground forces followed. The invasion was real. But its origins cannot be reduced to a single morning. To understand why two neighbouring states fought for eight years, we need to examine what each government said, what the documents establish, and what the war actually became.

beats.heading: THE BORDER
beats.text: At the centre of the dispute lay the Shatt al-Arab, the waterway linking Iraq's ports to the Gulf. In nineteen seventy-five, the Algiers Agreement attempted to settle a longstanding border conflict. Both governments later accused the other of violating the settlement.

beats.heading: AFTER THE REVOLUTION
beats.text: Iran's nineteen seventy-nine revolution brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power. His government's revolutionary language alarmed the Iraqi leadership. Baghdad feared subversion. Tehran accused Iraq of interfering with Iranian minorities and supporting opponents of the new republic. These were political accusations, not neutral findings.

beats.heading: THE PREWAR CLASHES
beats.text: There were real border clashes before the invasion. An Iraqi diplomatic account alleged shelling around Khanaqin and Mandali in early September nineteen eighty. Iranian diplomats presented their own accounts of Iraqi incursions. Documents reveal the positions of the governments. They do not, by themselves, prove every accusation.

beats.heading: SEPTEMBER 1980
beats.text: Saddam Hussein repudiated the Algiers Agreement in September. On the twenty-second, the Iraqi military launched a large offensive into Iran. Iraqi leaders expected a swift result. Instead, the fighting around Khorramshahr and Abadan drew both countries into a grinding war of attrition.

beats.heading: THE FIRST UN APPEAL
beats.text: Six days after the invasion, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution four hundred and seventy-nine. It called for an immediate end to further use of force and encouraged mediation. Iraq quickly indicated acceptance. Iranian officials were unwilling to accept a settlement on those terms while Iraqi troops remained on Iranian soil.

beats.heading: THE FIGHT FOR THE CITIES
beats.text: Khorramshahr became a symbol of the war's brutality. The initial Iraqi advance slowed. Iranian resistance stiffened around the occupied cities. Neither the Iraqi government's hope for a short campaign nor Iran's revolutionary confidence could overcome the realities of artillery, urban fighting and mass mobilisation.

beats.heading: THE TURNING POINT
beats.text: Iranian counteroffensives recovered much of the territory lost in nineteen eighty. On May twenty-fourth, nineteen eighty-two, Iran retook Khorramshahr. This changed the strategic balance. Iraq declared its readiness for a ceasefire, while the Iranian leadership chose to press on beyond the recovery of its territory.

beats.heading: WAR CROSSES THE FRONTIER
beats.text: From nineteen eighty-two, Iranian forces mounted offensives into Iraq. Baghdad now fought increasingly to prevent an Iranian breakthrough. Years of offensives and counteroffensives followed, with extraordinary losses but no lasting military decision.

beats.heading: A LONGER, DEADLIER WAR
beats.text: The conflict expanded beyond trenches. Cities were bombed. Oil infrastructure and shipping were attacked. Foreign governments supplied arms, finance or intelligence to one side or the other, often for conflicting strategic reasons. Neither Iraq nor Iran fought in isolation.

beats.heading: THE HUMAN RECORD
beats.text: The suffering cannot be measured only in lost ground. Civilians were displaced, prisoners were taken, and families on both sides endured years of fear. Iraq's use of chemical weapons, including against Kurdish civilians at Halabja in nineteen eighty-eight, remains one of the war's gravest crimes.

beats.heading: THE DIPLOMATIC EXIT
beats.text: In July nineteen eighty-seven the United Nations adopted Resolution five hundred and ninety-eight. It demanded a ceasefire, withdrawal to internationally recognised boundaries, prisoner exchanges, and a negotiated settlement. The diplomatic framework existed a year before the guns finally fell silent.

beats.heading: THE END
beats.text: Iran announced its acceptance of Resolution five hundred and ninety-eight in July nineteen eighty-eight. The ceasefire entered into force on August twentieth. Eight years after the first attacks, the two states faced an exhausted frontier and immense human loss.

beats.heading: THE HISTORICAL QUESTION
beats.text: The prewar clashes matter. The Iraqi and Iranian diplomatic claims deserve examination. So does the decision to continue the war after nineteen eighty-two. But those questions are not evidence that the September invasion never happened. The history is more difficult, and more revealing, than either government's wartime account.
